name: Liking Principle
description: People are more easily persuaded by, and more likely to comply with requests from, people they like -- including people they like for reasons unrelated to the request itself, such as fleeting attraction, flattery, similarity, or shared cooperative effort.
design_relevance_note: One of Cialdini's core persuasion principles, directly relevant to onboarding personas, chatbot/assistant tone, review and testimonial design, referral programs, and any flow that leans on a friendly, similar, or flattering presentation to increase compliance with a request (sign-ups, upsells, consent prompts).
prevalence_note: One of the most widely taught persuasion principles in marketing, sales, and CRO practice (via Cialdini's own popularization), though the underlying academic literature is less often traced back to by practitioners citing the principle by name.

findings.description: Across 98 studies yielding 251 findings, cooperation without intergroup competition produced greater interpersonal attraction than interpersonal competition, individualistic efforts, or cooperation paired with intergroup competition; even cooperation with intergroup competition still outperformed pure competition or working alone. In other words, working together is not just instrumentally effective — it reliably makes people like one another more.
findings.source_title: Interdependence and Interpersonal Attraction Among Heterogeneous and Homogeneous Individuals: A Theoretical Formulation and a Meta-analysis of the Research

findings.description: Across three studies, even brief or incidental attraction to a requester increased compliance with that person's request: a short conversation or simple co-presence raised agreement rates relative to no exposure, Study 2 reproduced the mere-exposure route while arguing against mood/priming alternatives, and Study 3 showed that perceived similarity to the requester also increased compliance. The paper's interpretation is that people can respond to fleeting attraction automatically, as if the requester were already a friend or long-term acquaintance.
findings.source_title: The Effect of Fleeting Attraction on Compliance to Requests

findings.description: Meta-analytic review of ingratiation research found that ingratiation tactics (including praise/flattery forms) have a small positive effect on performance evaluations but a significantly stronger positive effect on judgments of interpersonal attraction/liking, with the size of that benefit moderated by which ingratiation tactic is used, how transparent it appears, whether perceivers are the target or an observer, and the setting of the influence attempt.
findings.source_title: Impact of ingratiation on judgments and evaluations: A meta-analytic investigation.
findings.source_venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

applications.title: Amy's Kitchen's founder story making a shopper feel connected to a stranger's brand
applications.description: In an NN/g usability study, a participant visiting the Amy's Kitchen website said 'They make a nice pizza; I think she's local,' then spent several minutes reading the About Us section to learn more about 'Amy' -- despite Amy's Kitchen not actually being local to the participant, the personal founder story created a felt connection likely to influence a future purchase.
applications.ethical_note: A founder/origin story is a genuine, disclosed piece of brand information (not fabricated), and the liking it generates is based on real content the user chose to read -- distinct from liking-based tactics that manufacture a false sense of personal connection through fabricated details.

applications.title: Tupperware's home-party sales model: buying from a friend, not a store
applications.description: In the late 1940s, Tupperware moved from retail-only sales to hosted 'demonstration' home parties, where a host invited friends to view and buy products and earned a commission on sales -- by 1951, Tupperware had dropped retail outlets entirely because party sales, driven by guests' liking for the host rather than product need, generated far more revenue.
applications.ethical_note: Guests reported buying items 'not because they needed or wanted them' but out of liking for the host and a sense of obligation to help her earn commission -- a real tension between genuine social liking and purchases made against the buyer's own stated interest, the same dynamic that makes modern 'friend referral' and social-commerce features (this graph's own Rue La La-style patterns) worth scrutinizing rather than treating liking-driven conversion as automatically benign.
